text.preview: 'NAGLALARO AKO NG CALL OF DUTY, HINDI KO NAISIP KAILANMAN NA MAMARIL SA LABAS' The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City. Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence. "Naglalaro ako ng Call of Duty, hindi ko naisip kailanman na mamaril sa labas. Maraming pag-aaral ang ginawa na nagpapatunay na walang matibay na ebidensya na nagsasabing ang video game ay may direktang dahilan sa school violence o crime in real life," Samaniego said. He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use. "Ang tunay na dahilan nun hindi 'yung laro, kundi 'yung mga taong nakakausap nung bata online. Ang dapat nating gawin hindi i-ban 'yung game, kundi tingnan ang kabuuang isyu," Samaniego said. He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option. Samaniego said the real enforcement gap is not the existence of violent games but the failure to implement existing age ratings—GoreBox is an 18+ game that a 14-year-old was able to access—drawing a direct comparison to the MTRCB film rating system. output.preview:
'I AM PLAYING CALL OF DUTY, I NEVER THOUGHT OF SHOOTING OUTSIDE'
The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City.
Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence.
"I am playing Call of Duty, I never thought of shooting outside. Many studies have been done proving that there is no solid evidence saying that video games directly cause school violence or crime in real life," Samaniego said.
He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use.
"The real reason is not the game, but the people the child was talking to online. What we should do is not ban the game, but look at the overall issue," Samaniego said.
He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option.
Samaniego said the real enforcement gap is not the existence of violent games but the failure to implement existing age ratings—GoreBox is an 18+ game that a 14-year-old was able to access—drawing a direct comparison to the MTRCB film rating system.
"It’s like with the MTRCB, there is a rating. If MTRCB has a film made by Vivamax and a 12-year-old watched it, are we going to shut down Vivamax? Or will we look at why they got into the cinema due

The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City.
Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence.
"I am playing Call of Duty, I never thought of shooting outside. Many studies have been done proving that there is no solid evidence saying that video games directly cause school violence or crime in real life," Samaniego said.
He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use.
"The real reason is not the game, but the people the child was talking to online. What we should do is not ban the game, but look at the overall issue," Samaniego said.
He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option.
Samaniego said the real enforcement gap is not the existence of violent games but the failure to implement existing age ratings—GoreBox is an 18+ game that a 14-year-old was able to access—drawing a direct comparison to the MTRCB film rating system.

segments: 'I AM PLAYING CALL OF DUTY, I NEVER THOUGHT OF SHOOTING OUTSIDE'

The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City.

Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence.

"I am playing Call of Duty, I never thought of shooting outside. Many studies have been done proving that there is no solid evidence saying that video games directly cause school violence or crime in real life," Samaniego said.

He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use.
"The real reason is not the game, but the people the child was talking to online. What we should do is not ban the game, but look at the overall issue," Samaniego said.

He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option.

Samaniego said the real enforcement gap is not the existence of violent games but the failure to implement existing age ratings—GoreBox is an 18+ game that a 14-year-old was able to access—drawing a direct comparison to the MTRCB film rating system.

"It’s like with the MTRCB, there is a rating. If MTRCB has a film made by Vivamax and a 12-year-old watched it, are we going to shut down Vivamax? Or will we look at why they got into the cinema due to wrong implementation? That’s what lawmakers should think," Samaniego said.

output.title: What is GoreBox, the video game linked to one of the Tacloban school shooting suspects?
output.description: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.

text.preview: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. The shooting incident left three students dead, 15 wounded, and five more with non-firearm-related injuries. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox. What is Gorebox? According to the official Steam page, GoreBox is a physics-driven sandbox game developed by Felix Filip and published by F2 Games. The game was released on Steam on July 21, 2023, and features a tool called the “Reality Crusher,” which allows players to spawn, manipulate, and destroy objects within the game world. Known for its graphic depictions of violence, it offers players the opportunity to explore diverse environments and experiment with a variety of weapons, tools, and explosives in a highly interactive sandbox setting. Temporary ban The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Tuesday has ordered the temporary ban of Gorebox following the shooting incident in Tacloban. "Base din po sa pag-interview ng mga investigators natin, talagang napagplanuhan as early as May 1 or April na mag-launch sila ng ganitong ano, kaya talagang premeditated 'yung incident," he said. output.description: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.
output.text: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox, a sandbox-style game that allows players to create and destroy objects and simulate chaos using various weapons. Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News

output.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
output.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. The post, first published by Malacañang Republic (May 17, 2026) and shared by an FB user and FB pages SK Memes (July 17, 2023) and EXG Boss L.A. (July 8, 2019), has garnered a cumulative 243,700 reactions, 32,000 comments and 219,000 shares, as of writing. E

As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. output.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
output.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. When news of the Tacloban shooting broke, he said, his first questions were whether the attackers were gamers and whether the case was tied to 764, both of which, he said, appeared to hold up. output.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
output.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are

text.preview: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence.

'I AM PLAYING CALL OF DUTY, I NEVER THOUGHT OF SHOOTING OUTSIDE'
The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City.
Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence.
"I am playing Call of Duty, I never thought of shooting outside. Many studies have been done proving that there is no solid evidence saying that video games directly cause school violence or crime in real life," Samaniego said.
He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use.
"The real reason is not the game, but the people the child was talking to online. What we should do is not ban the game, but look at the overall issue," Samaniego said.
He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option.
Samaniego said the real enforcement gap is not the existence of violent games but the failure to implement existing age ratings—GoreBox is an 18+ game that a 14-year-old was able to access—drawing a direct comparison to the MTRCB film rating system.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
articles.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. The post, first published by Malacañang Republic (May 17, 2026) and shared by an FB user and FB pages SK Memes (July 17, 2023) and EXG Boss L.A. (July 8, 2019), has garnered a cumulative 243,700 reactions, 32,000 comments and 219,000 shares, as of writing. E

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
articles.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. The post, first published by Malacañang Republic (May 17, 2026) and shared by an FB user and FB pages SK Memes (July 17, 2023) and EXG Boss L.A. articles.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
articles.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are

text.preview: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence.

The shooting incident left three students dead, 15 wounded, and five more with non-firearm-related injuries. Known for its graphic depictions of violence, it offers players the opportunity to explore diverse environments and experiment with a variety of weapons, tools, and explosives in a highly interactive sandbox setting. articles.title: Tacloban shooting suspect's violent behavior linked to online game GoreBox
articles.description: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.
articles.text: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox, a sandbox-style game that allows players to create and destroy objects and simulate chaos using various weapons. Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News

articles.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
articles.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. When news of the Tacloban shooting broke, he said, his first questions were whether the attackers were gamers and whether the case was tied to 764, both of which, he said, appeared to hold up. articles.title: Police link Tacloban campus shooter to violent mobile game
articles.description: Police said one of the minors in the Tacloban school shooting had a history of playing a game described as violent.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — One of the minors in the Tacloban City school shooting had a history of playing a game described by police as violent, the Eastern Visayas police said Tuesday, June 23. In a phone interview with reporters, Police Regional Office 8 Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy said investigators found that one of the suspects played a game called "Gorebox." "Just like the Roblox, may laro. May shooting, shooting din. May ganoong firearm. Medyo bayolente yung laro," Capoy said. (Just like Roblox, there is a game. There is also shooting. There is that kind of firearm. The game is somewhat violent.) Capoy said the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game. According to descriptions on gaming platforms Steam and Google Play, "Gorebox"—which is rated for gamers aged 18 and above—is a "chaotic physics-driven sandbox where creativity meets destruction." Capoy said one of the underage suspects had basic knowledge of firearm handling from a previous visit to a shooting range, including how to release and reload a magazine. Investigators also flagged viral screenshots of text messages allegedly involving the suspects, which Capoy said suggested they had studied the crime and read up on the law. "Napakabilis ng pagkalat ng mga screenshot doon sa text messages nila. Nakakabahala din dahil parang may alam sila. Inaral din nila. Nagbabasa din ng batas," Capoy said. (The screenshots of their text messages spread incredibly fast. It is also alarming because it seems they knew something. They studied it and were also reading the law.) As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. Three people were killed in the shooting. Capoy said the aunt of one of the suspects, a police officer, has been placed under restrictive custody . articles.description: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.
articles.text: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox, a sandbox-style game that allows players to create and destroy objects and simulate chaos using various weapons. Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News

articles.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
articles.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. articles.title: Police link Tacloban campus shooter to violent mobile game
articles.description: Police said one of the minors in the Tacloban school shooting had a history of playing a game described as violent.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — One of the minors in the Tacloban City school shooting had a history of playing a game described by police as violent, the Eastern Visayas police said Tuesday, June 23. In a phone interview with reporters, Police Regional Office 8 Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy said investigators found that one of the suspects played a game called "Gorebox." "Just like the Roblox, may laro. May shooting, shooting din. May ganoong firearm. Medyo bayolente yung laro," Capoy said. (Just like Roblox, there is a game. There is also shooting. There is that kind of firearm. The game is somewhat violent.) Capoy said the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game. According to descriptions on gaming platforms Steam and Google Play, "Gorebox"—which is rated for gamers aged 18 and above—is a "chaotic physics-driven sandbox where creativity meets destruction." Capoy said one of the underage suspects had basic knowledge of firearm handling from a previous visit to a shooting range, including how to release and reload a magazine. Investigators also flagged viral screenshots of text messages allegedly involving the suspects, which Capoy said suggested they had studied the crime and read up on the law. "Napakabilis ng pagkalat ng mga screenshot doon sa text messages nila. Nakakabahala din dahil parang may alam sila. Inaral din nila. Nagbabasa din ng batas," Capoy said. (The screenshots of their text messages spread incredibly fast. It is also alarming because it seems they knew something. They studied it and were also reading the law.) As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. Three people were killed in the shooting. Capoy said the aunt of one of the suspects, a police officer, has been placed under restrictive custody . evidence_context.preview:
'I AM PLAYING CALL OF DUTY, I NEVER THOUGHT OF SHOOTING OUTSIDE'
The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City.
Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence.
"I am playing Call of Duty, I never thought of shooting outside. Many studies have been done proving that there is no solid evidence saying that video games directly cause school violence or crime in real life," Samaniego said.
He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use.
"The real reason is not the game, but the people the child was talking to online. What we should do is not ban the game, but look at the overall issue," Samaniego said.
He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option.
Samaniego said the real enforcement gap is not the existence of violent games but the failure to implement existing age ratings—GoreBox is an 18+ game that a 14-year-old was able to access—drawing a direct comparison to the MTRCB film rating system.
"It’s like with the MTRCB, there is a rating. If MTRCB has a film made by Vivamax and a 12-year-old watched it, are we going to shut down Vivamax? Or will we look at why they got into the cinema due

article.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
article.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are

text.preview: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence.

article.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
article.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. The post, first published by Malacañang Republic (May 17, 2026) and shared by an FB user and FB pages SK Memes (July 17, 2023) and EXG Boss L.A. (July 8, 2019), has garnered a cumulative 243,700 reactions, 32,000 comments and 219,000 shares, as of writing. E

article.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
article.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are

text.preview: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence.

article.title: What is GoreBox, the video game linked to one of the Tacloban school shooting suspects?
article.description: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.

text.preview: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. The shooting incident left three students dead, 15 wounded, and five more with non-firearm-related injuries. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox. What is Gorebox? According to the official Steam page, GoreBox is a physics-driven sandbox game developed by Felix Filip and published by F2 Games. The game was released on Steam on July 21, 2023, and features a tool called the “Reality Crusher,” which allows players to spawn, manipulate, and destroy objects within the game world. Known for its graphic depictions of violence, it offers players the opportunity to explore diverse environments and experiment with a variety of weapons, tools, and explosives in a highly interactive sandbox setting. Temporary ban The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Tuesday has ordered the temporary ban of Gorebox following the shooting incident in Tacloban. In an interview on " Balitanghali " on Tuesday, Capoy also noted that the school shooting was premeditated and that one of the suspects allegedly claimed he and his companion only wanted to scare other students. "Base din po sa pag-interview ng mga investigators natin, talagang napagplanuhan as early as May 1 or April na mag-launch sila ng ganitong ano, kaya talagang premeditated 'yung incident," he said. article.title: Tacloban shooting suspect's violent behavior linked to online game GoreBox
article.description: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.
article.text: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox, a sandbox-style game that allows players to create and destroy objects and simulate chaos using various weapons. Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News

article.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
article.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. When news of the Tacloban shooting broke, he said, his first questions were whether the attackers were gamers and whether the case was tied to 764, both of which, he said, appeared to hold up. article.title: Police link Tacloban campus shooter to violent mobile game
article.description: Police said one of the minors in the Tacloban school shooting had a history of playing a game described as violent.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — One of the minors in the Tacloban City school shooting had a history of playing a game described by police as violent, the Eastern Visayas police said Tuesday, June 23. In a phone interview with reporters, Police Regional Office 8 Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy said investigators found that one of the suspects played a game called "Gorebox." "Just like the Roblox, may laro. May shooting, shooting din. May ganoong firearm. Medyo bayolente yung laro," Capoy said. (Just like Roblox, there is a game. There is also shooting. There is that kind of firearm. The game is somewhat violent.) Capoy said the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game. According to descriptions on gaming platforms Steam and Google Play, "Gorebox"—which is rated for gamers aged 18 and above—is a "chaotic physics-driven sandbox where creativity meets destruction." Capoy said one of the underage suspects had basic knowledge of firearm handling from a previous visit to a shooting range, including how to release and reload a magazine. Investigators also flagged viral screenshots of text messages allegedly involving the suspects, which Capoy said suggested they had studied the crime and read up on the law. "Napakabilis ng pagkalat ng mga screenshot doon sa text messages nila. Nakakabahala din dahil parang may alam sila. Inaral din nila. Nagbabasa din ng batas," Capoy said. (The screenshots of their text messages spread incredibly fast. It is also alarming because it seems they knew something. They studied it and were also reading the law.) As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. Three people were killed in the shooting. Capoy said the aunt of one of the suspects, a police officer, has been placed under restrictive custody . article.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
article.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. article.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
article.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are

text.preview: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence.

article.title: What is GoreBox, the video game linked to one of the Tacloban school shooting suspects?
article.description: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.

text.preview: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. The shooting incident left three students dead, 15 wounded, and five more with non-firearm-related injuries. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox. What is Gorebox? According to the official Steam page, GoreBox is a physics-driven sandbox game developed by Felix Filip and published by F2 Games. The game was released on Steam on July 21, 2023, and features a tool called the “Reality Crusher,” which allows players to spawn, manipulate, and destroy objects within the game world. Known for its graphic depictions of violence, it offers players the opportunity to explore diverse environments and experiment with a variety of weapons, tools, and explosives in a highly interactive sandbox setting. Temporary ban The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Tuesday has ordered the temporary ban of Gorebox following the shooting incident in Tacloban. In an interview on " Balitanghali " on Tuesday, Capoy also noted that the school shooting was premeditated and that one of the suspects allegedly claimed he and his companion only wanted to scare other students. "Base din po sa pag-interview ng mga investigators natin, talagang napagplanuhan as early as May 1 or April na mag-launch sila ng ganitong ano, kaya talagang premeditated 'yung incident," he said. article.title: Tacloban shooting suspect's violent behavior linked to online game GoreBox
article.description: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.
article.text: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox, a sandbox-style game that allows players to create and destroy objects and simulate chaos using various weapons. Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News

article.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
article.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. When news of the Tacloban shooting broke, he said, his first questions were whether the attackers were gamers and whether the case was tied to 764, both of which, he said, appeared to hold up. article.title: Police link Tacloban campus shooter to violent mobile game
article.description: Police said one of the minors in the Tacloban school shooting had a history of playing a game described as violent.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — One of the minors in the Tacloban City school shooting had a history of playing a game described by police as violent, the Eastern Visayas police said Tuesday, June 23. In a phone interview with reporters, Police Regional Office 8 Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy said investigators found that one of the suspects played a game called "Gorebox." "Just like the Roblox, may laro. May shooting, shooting din. May ganoong firearm. Medyo bayolente yung laro," Capoy said. (Just like Roblox, there is a game. There is also shooting. There is that kind of firearm. The game is somewhat violent.) Capoy said the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game. According to descriptions on gaming platforms Steam and Google Play, "Gorebox"—which is rated for gamers aged 18 and above—is a "chaotic physics-driven sandbox where creativity meets destruction." Capoy said one of the underage suspects had basic knowledge of firearm handling from a previous visit to a shooting range, including how to release and reload a magazine. Investigators also flagged viral screenshots of text messages allegedly involving the suspects, which Capoy said suggested they had studied the crime and read up on the law. "Napakabilis ng pagkalat ng mga screenshot doon sa text messages nila. Nakakabahala din dahil parang may alam sila. Inaral din nila. Nagbabasa din ng batas," Capoy said. (The screenshots of their text messages spread incredibly fast. It is also alarming because it seems they knew something. They studied it and were also reading the law.) As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. Three people were killed in the shooting. Capoy said the aunt of one of the suspects, a police officer, has been placed under restrictive custody . 'I AM PLAYING CALL OF DUTY, I NEVER THOUGHT OF SHOOTING OUTSIDE'
The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City.
Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence.
"I am playing Call of Duty, I never thought of shooting outside. Many studies have been done proving that there is no solid evidence saying that video games directly cause school violence or crime in real life," Samaniego said.
He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use.
"The real reason is not the game, but the people the child was talking to online. What we should do is not ban the game, but look at the overall issue," Samaniego said.
He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option.
Samaniego said the real enforcement gap is not the existence of violent games but the failure to implement existing age ratings—GoreBox is an 18+ game that a 14-year-old was able to access—drawing a direct comparison to the MTRCB film rating system.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
articles.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. articles.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
articles.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are

text.preview: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence.

text.preview: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. The shooting incident left three students dead, 15 wounded, and five more with non-firearm-related injuries. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox. What is Gorebox? According to the official Steam page, GoreBox is a physics-driven sandbox game developed by Felix Filip and published by F2 Games. The game was released on Steam on July 21, 2023, and features a tool called the “Reality Crusher,” which allows players to spawn, manipulate, and destroy objects within the game world. Known for its graphic depictions of violence, it offers players the opportunity to explore diverse environments and experiment with a variety of weapons, tools, and explosives in a highly interactive sandbox setting. Temporary ban The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Tuesday has ordered the temporary ban of Gorebox following the shooting incident in Tacloban. "Base din po sa pag-interview ng mga investigators natin, talagang napagplanuhan as early as May 1 or April na mag-launch sila ng ganitong ano, kaya talagang premeditated 'yung incident," he said. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox, a sandbox-style game that allows players to create and destroy objects and simulate chaos using various weapons. Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News
