articles.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
articles.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. When news of the Tacloban shooting broke, he said, his first questions were whether the attackers were gamers and whether the case was tied to 764, both of which, he said, appeared to hold up. articles.title: Police link Tacloban campus shooter to violent mobile game
articles.description: Police said one of the minors in the Tacloban school shooting had a history of playing a game described as violent.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — One of the minors in the Tacloban City school shooting had a history of playing a game described by police as violent, the Eastern Visayas police said Tuesday, June 23. In a phone interview with reporters, Police Regional Office 8 Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy said investigators found that one of the suspects played a game called "Gorebox." "Just like the Roblox, may laro. May shooting, shooting din. May ganoong firearm. Medyo bayolente yung laro," Capoy said. (Just like Roblox, there is a game. There is also shooting. There is that kind of firearm. The game is somewhat violent.) Capoy said the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game. According to descriptions on gaming platforms Steam and Google Play, "Gorebox"—which is rated for gamers aged 18 and above—is a "chaotic physics-driven sandbox where creativity meets destruction." Capoy said one of the underage suspects had basic knowledge of firearm handling from a previous visit to a shooting range, including how to release and reload a magazine. Investigators also flagged viral screenshots of text messages allegedly involving the suspects, which Capoy said suggested they had studied the crime and read up on the law. "Napakabilis ng pagkalat ng mga screenshot doon sa text messages nila. Nakakabahala din dahil parang may alam sila. Inaral din nila. Nagbabasa din ng batas," Capoy said. (The screenshots of their text messages spread incredibly fast. It is also alarming because it seems they knew something. They studied it and were also reading the law.) As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. Three people were killed in the shooting. Capoy said the aunt of one of the suspects, a police officer, has been placed under restrictive custody . The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. articles.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
articles.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. The post, first published by Malacañang Republic (May 17, 2026) and shared by an FB user and FB pages SK Memes (July 17, 2023) and EXG Boss L.A. (July 8, 2019), has garnered a cumulative 243,700 reactions, 32,000 comments and 219,000 shares, as of writing. E

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
articles.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.

text.preview: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. articles.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
articles.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. 'I AM PLAYING CALL OF DUTY, I NEVER THOUGHT OF SHOOTING OUTSIDE'
The rush to blame video games for school violence is not supported by science, a cybersecurity and technology expert said Saturday, pushing back against calls to ban video games in the wake of a shooting incident involving a minor in Tacloban City.
Cybersecurity and technology expert Art Samaniego Jr. made the argument in an interview on DZRH News program "Special on Saturday" on July 4, citing research by the Oxford Internet Institute showing no direct link between violent video games and real-world crime or violence.
"I am playing Call of Duty, I never thought of shooting outside. Many studies have been done proving that there is no solid evidence saying that video games directly cause school violence or crime in real life," Samaniego said.
He said the real cause of the Tacloban school shooting was not GoreBox—the game the 14-year-old shooter allegedly played—but the people the child was communicating with online, and that extremist recruiters and online predators follow children across platforms regardless of which game or app they use.
"The real reason is not the game, but the people the child was talking to online. What we should do is not ban the game, but look at the overall issue," Samaniego said.
He warned that banning GoreBox specifically is futile since more than 20 similar games exist on mobile platforms alone, and more on PC and console—and children, he said, have no loyalty to specific platforms and will simply migrate to the next available option.

A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. The post, first published by Malacañang Republic (May 17, 2026) and shared by an FB user and FB pages SK Memes (July 17, 2023) and EXG Boss L.A. article.description: A shooting incident was reported at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, Leyte on Monday morning.

text.preview: A video shared with ABS-CBN News showed students and teachers rushing out of the school, some of them weeping. A female student who appeared to be wounded was carried outside by her peers . The alleged shooters, aged 15 and 14, had fired "randomly" inside San Jose National High School, PLt. Evalyn Diaz told AFP of the violence that sent terrified students running for cover. Irvin Nogar, a 52-year-old social studies teacher, told AFP he was in the middle of a class at the school in Leyte province's Tacloban City when he heard several "loud gun shots". "I saw a shooter walking towards our area, so I told the students to be calm and hide under their desks and I locked the door... they were crying and in panic." A video shared with ABS-CBN News showed panicked children screaming and crying while hiding inside a classroom amid the sound of gunfire. In another video, students and teachers rushed out of the school, some of them weeping. A female student who appeared to be wounded was carried outside by her peers. The fatalities were confirmed to be students. Police said the 2 suspects in the shooting have been arrested, including a Grade 9 student from the same school. Jennelyn Badoria, mother of a slain 15-year-old student, told AFP she believed whoever had given the shooters access to guns must be held accountable. "I'm asking that the gun owners be charged, because the guns wouldn't have ended up in the children’s hands if it weren't for them," she said in an interview outside the school. article.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
article.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are

text.preview: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence.

article.title: What is GoreBox, the video game linked to one of the Tacloban school shooting suspects?
article.description: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.

text.preview: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. The shooting incident left three students dead, 15 wounded, and five more with non-firearm-related injuries. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox. What is Gorebox? According to the official Steam page, GoreBox is a physics-driven sandbox game developed by Felix Filip and published by F2 Games. The game was released on Steam on July 21, 2023, and features a tool called the “Reality Crusher,” which allows players to spawn, manipulate, and destroy objects within the game world. Known for its graphic depictions of violence, it offers players the opportunity to explore diverse environments and experiment with a variety of weapons, tools, and explosives in a highly interactive sandbox setting. Temporary ban The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Tuesday has ordered the temporary ban of Gorebox following the shooting incident in Tacloban. In an interview on " Balitanghali " on Tuesday, Capoy also noted that the school shooting was premeditated and that one of the suspects allegedly claimed he and his companion only wanted to scare other students. "Base din po sa pag-interview ng mga investigators natin, talagang napagplanuhan as early as May 1 or April na mag-launch sila ng ganitong ano, kaya talagang premeditated 'yung incident," he said. article.title: Tacloban shooting suspect's violent behavior linked to online game GoreBox
article.description: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.
article.text: The Philippine National Police is looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in Monday's fatal shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox, a sandbox-style game that allows players to create and destroy objects and simulate chaos using various weapons. Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News

article.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
article.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. When news of the Tacloban shooting broke, he said, his first questions were whether the attackers were gamers and whether the case was tied to 764, both of which, he said, appeared to hold up. article.title: Police link Tacloban campus shooter to violent mobile game
article.description: Police said one of the minors in the Tacloban school shooting had a history of playing a game described as violent.

text.preview: MANILA, Philippines — One of the minors in the Tacloban City school shooting had a history of playing a game described by police as violent, the Eastern Visayas police said Tuesday, June 23. In a phone interview with reporters, Police Regional Office 8 Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy said investigators found that one of the suspects played a game called "Gorebox." "Just like the Roblox, may laro. May shooting, shooting din. May ganoong firearm. Medyo bayolente yung laro," Capoy said. (Just like Roblox, there is a game. There is also shooting. There is that kind of firearm. The game is somewhat violent.) Capoy said the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game. According to descriptions on gaming platforms Steam and Google Play, "Gorebox"—which is rated for gamers aged 18 and above—is a "chaotic physics-driven sandbox where creativity meets destruction." Capoy said one of the underage suspects had basic knowledge of firearm handling from a previous visit to a shooting range, including how to release and reload a magazine. Investigators also flagged viral screenshots of text messages allegedly involving the suspects, which Capoy said suggested they had studied the crime and read up on the law. "Napakabilis ng pagkalat ng mga screenshot doon sa text messages nila. Nakakabahala din dahil parang may alam sila. Inaral din nila. Nagbabasa din ng batas," Capoy said. (The screenshots of their text messages spread incredibly fast. It is also alarming because it seems they knew something. They studied it and were also reading the law.) As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. Three people were killed in the shooting. Capoy said the aunt of one of the suspects, a police officer, has been placed under restrictive custody . output.title: What is GoreBox, the video game linked to one of the Tacloban school shooting suspects?
output.description: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox.
output.text: The Philippine National Police is now looking into the possibility that the violent behavior of one of the two minor suspects in the shooting incident in San Jose National High School in Barangay San Jose, Tacloban City, on Monday may have been influenced by the online game GoreBox. The shooting incident left three students dead, 15 wounded, and five more with non-firearm-related injuries. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. In an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Tuesday, Police Brig. Gen. Jayson Capoy, director of the Police Regional Office in Eastern Visayas, said the 14-year-old suspect had been playing GoreBox. What is Gorebox? According to the official Steam page, GoreBox is a physics-driven sandbox game developed by Felix Filip and published by F2 Games. The game was released on Steam on July 21, 2023, and features a tool called the “Reality Crusher,” which allows players to spawn, manipulate, and destroy objects within the game world. Known for its graphic depictions of violence, it offers players the opportunity to explore diverse environments and experiment with a variety of weapons, tools, and explosives in a highly interactive sandbox setting. Temporary ban The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) on Tuesday has ordered the temporary ban of Gorebox following the shooting incident in Tacloban. In an interview on " Balitanghali " on Tuesday, Capoy also noted that the school shooting was premeditated and that one of the suspects allegedly claimed he and his companion only wanted to scare other students. "Base din po sa pag-interview ng mga investigators natin, talagang napagplanuhan as early as May 1 or April na mag-launch sila ng ganitong ano, kaya talagang premeditated 'yung incident," he said. The Department of Education (DepEd) suspended classes in all schools in Tacloban on Tuesday following the shooting incident. Psychological first aid (PFA) will be conducted from June 24 to 26, per DepEd's directive. —CDC GMA News

Investigators are also looking into reports that the attack may have been rooted in bullying, based on the suspects’ initial statements. Capoy clarified that the death toll remained at three, while 20 others were injured. Of the injured, 15 sustained gunshot wounds, while the rest were hurt while trying to escape, police said. The two suspects, aged 14 and 15, both Grade 9 students and reportedly close friends, allegedly entered two classrooms and opened fire on their schoolmates before they were arrested. Police recovered a Glock pistol and a .38-caliber revolver from the scene. One of the firearms was reportedly issued to a police officer relative, who is now under investigation. The Department of Education has since coordinated with local authorities and social welfare agencies to provide medical and psychosocial support to affected students and school personnel. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a full investigation and heightened security measures in schools and other public areas. —MCG GMA News

output.title: 3 dead, 13 injured in school shooting in Tacloban | ABS-CBN News
output.description: A shooting incident was reported at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, Leyte on Monday morning.
output.text: A video shared with ABS-CBN News showed students and teachers rushing out of the school, some of them weeping. A female student who appeared to be wounded was carried outside by her peers . Contributed via Jeanette Ruedas MANILA (2nd UPDATE) — Three teenagers were killed while 13 others were injured when two students opened fire at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, Leyte on Monday morning, police said. The alleged shooters, aged 15 and 14, had fired "randomly" inside San Jose National High School, PLt. Evalyn Diaz told AFP of the violence that sent terrified students running for cover. Irvin Nogar, a 52-year-old social studies teacher, told AFP he was in the middle of a class at the school in Leyte province's Tacloban City when he heard several "loud gun shots". "I saw a shooter walking towards our area, so I told the students to be calm and hide under their desks and I locked the door... they were crying and in panic." A video shared with ABS-CBN News showed panicked children screaming and crying while hiding inside a classroom amid the sound of gunfire. In another video, students and teachers rushed out of the school, some of them weeping. A female student who appeared to be wounded was carried outside by her peers. The fatalities were confirmed to be students. Police said the 2 suspects in the shooting have been arrested, including a Grade 9 student from the same school. Jennelyn Badoria, mother of a slain 15-year-old student, told AFP she believed whoever had given the shooters access to guns must be held accountable. "I'm asking that the gun owners be charged, because the guns wouldn't have ended up in the children’s hands if it weren't for them," she said in an interview outside the school. Diaz, the police lieutenant, said they had heard "bullying was the motive", but that the two alleged shooters were still being interrogated. "We're still getting the guns, checking where they got those, and how they were able to bring that inside the school," she said. "They are still in the police station undergoing questioning in the presence of their parents because they are minors." A 2022 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development report found over half of Filipino boys and 43 percent of girls reported being bullied "at least a few times a month" -- more than double the rate of OECD countries. ‘HIGH-ALERT SITUATION’ Police investigators walk in front of the school entrance after a shooting incident at a high school compound in Tacloban City, Leyte province on June 22, 2026. Noel Sianosa, AFP President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ordered a thorough investigation into the incident, Malacanang said. “Kinakalungkot ng Pangulo ang pangyayari. Kahit sino pa man lalo na ang mga magulang ng mga nabiktima ay makakaramdam ang lungkot at takot,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said. The Department of Education classified the shooting as a “high-alert situation” and said its personnel were “coordinating closely with school authorities and law enforcement.” “To address the immediate emotional toll of this tragedy, the Department is working hand-in-hand with relevant government agencies to deploy critical medical assistance and appropriate psychosocial interventions for the affected learners and personnel,” the agency said. “We strongly condemn this act of violence and extend our deepest condolences to the families of the victims, as well as our earnest prayers for the swift recovery of those who were injured. The Central Office is now mobilizing assistance to our affected learners.” DepEd urged the public “to respect the privacy and dignity of all children involved and to allow the proper authorities to conduct a thorough and impartial inquiry.” “The safety, well-being, and mental health of our learners and personnel remain among the Department’s highest and most uncompromisable priorities. We remain committed to ensuring that our schools are secure, supportive environments for all,” it said. The Department of Justice said officials of the Tacloban City Police Office and the Office of the City Prosecutor of Tacloban are in coordination with each other on the on-going investigation on the shooting incident in San Jose National High School. The DOJ said in a statement that authorities are currently gathering all material details, including identities of the victims and the persons allegedly involved as well as the circumstances and possible motive behind the incident. "The Department will allow law enforcement authorities and the prosecutors concerned to complete their investigation, subject to all applicable safeguards under the law, especially those involving children in conflict with the law," the DOJ said. The DOJ added it is in coordination with the Office of the Regional Prosecutor of Region VIII to determine the facts on the shooting incident. In a statement, the Tacloban City Police Office (TCPO) said it strongly condemns the shooting incident. "At present, law enforcement authorities are conducting an extensive investigation to determine the circumstances surrounding the incident, identify all persons involved, and establish the motive behind this unfortunate event. Appropriate police operations are likewise being undertaken to are held accountable under the full force of the law," the police said. A quarter century of deadly gun violence in US schools Classes in Tacloban's San Jose Central School and Manlurip Elementary School have been suspended. While school shootings are a rarity in the Philippines, targeted gun violence is a fixture of provincial politics. In 2022, three people, including a former city mayor, were killed in a shooting incident before a graduation ceremony at Ateneo de Manila University. It was later determined to have been an assassination driven by "personal motives". Legal gun ownership is tightly regulated in the country, but a large black market exists for firearms. -- with a report from Adrian Ayalin, ABS-CBN News This is a developing story. output.title: FACT CHECK: Viral list of online games banned for being violent SATIRE
output.description: Neither the national government nor any local government unit released an official list of banned violent online games. The viral photo claiming that 43 games had been banned is satirical.
output.text: The government released an official list of 43 online games banned for being “violent.” The graphic listing online games is labeled as satire. The original creator of the graphic is a satire and parody Facebook page. A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims that the Philippine government has released an official list of online games banned for being “violent.” This is satire. On June 27, an FB page posted a graphic of a list of 43 popular video games, including Minecraft, Mobile Legends, Roblox, Fortnite and Candy Crush. It carried the text: “Games that are too violent and should be banned forthwith according to LGU.” “JUST IN: Several Lawmakers supports (sic) this ban.” On the lower right corner of the image was a “satire” label. The following day, the post was taken down, but by then it had been re-posted by two FB pages and an FB user. One of them included a caption which read: “Wait.. totoo ba to? DOTA too cool for the kids? Or di nila naiintindihan yung game kasi too complex? Lol (Wait, is this true? Is DOTA too cool for the kids? Or do they not understand the game because it’s too complex? Lol).” The original publisher re-posted the online games list on July 1, and it continues to gain views and engagements. The page is known for satire and parody, and has a significant following. The disinformation surfaced after the Department of the Interior and Local Government flagged violent video games as potentially harmful to young people, following the June 22 school shooting in Tacloban City carried out by students, aged 14 and 15. The number of online games in the list is exaggerated, and even with some of these noted to be violent, long-time gamers argue playing has not influenced them to behave viciously. The post, first published by Malacañang Republic (May 17, 2026) and shared by an FB user and FB pages SK Memes (July 17, 2023) and EXG Boss L.A. (July 8, 2019), has garnered a cumulative 243,700 reactions, 32,000 comments and 219,000 shares, as of writing. Editor’s note: This fact check was produced with the help of a journalism student from the University of the Philippines Diliman as part of their internship at VERA Files. output.title: Police link Tacloban campus shooter to violent mobile game
output.description: Police said one of the minors in the Tacloban school shooting had a history of playing a game described as violent.
output.text: MANILA, Philippines — One of the minors in the Tacloban City school shooting had a history of playing a game described by police as violent, the Eastern Visayas police said Tuesday, June 23. In a phone interview with reporters, Police Regional Office 8 Director Brig. Gen. Jason Capoy said investigators found that one of the suspects played a game called "Gorebox." "Just like the Roblox, may laro. May shooting, shooting din. May ganoong firearm. Medyo bayolente yung laro," Capoy said. (Just like Roblox, there is a game. There is also shooting. There is that kind of firearm. The game is somewhat violent.) Capoy said the 14-year-old suspect was the one who played the game. According to descriptions on gaming platforms Steam and Google Play, "Gorebox"—which is rated for gamers aged 18 and above—is a "chaotic physics-driven sandbox where creativity meets destruction." Capoy said one of the underage suspects had basic knowledge of firearm handling from a previous visit to a shooting range, including how to release and reload a magazine. Investigators also flagged viral screenshots of text messages allegedly involving the suspects, which Capoy said suggested they had studied the crime and read up on the law. "Napakabilis ng pagkalat ng mga screenshot doon sa text messages nila. Nakakabahala din dahil parang may alam sila. Inaral din nila. Nagbabasa din ng batas," Capoy said. (The screenshots of their text messages spread incredibly fast. It is also alarming because it seems they knew something. They studied it and were also reading the law.) As of 8 a.m. on June 23, the Tacloban City local government, citing the PNP, said 15 people suffered gunshot wounds while five others sustained non-gunshot injuries. Three people were killed in the shooting. Capoy said the aunt of one of the suspects, a police officer, has been placed under restrictive custody . output.title: Tacloban shooting may be first 'completed' attack by 764 extremist network — expert
output.description: The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1.
output.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Tacloban school shooting may be the first mass shooting the online extremist network 764 carried out to completion anywhere in the world, a cybersecurity expert told senators on Wednesday, July 1. Angel Redoble, chair of the Philippine Institute of Cyber Security Professionals, shared his assessment at the Senate panel's first hearing on the June 22 attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban. The same hearing also saw the Philippine National Police (PNP) disclose that it has rescued at least 24 minors part of the same broad online network since October 2025. Five of the children rescued were found to have harmed themselves. "The first completed mass shooting, if we can finally attribute that to 764, that will be the first," Redoble said. "Because in 2025 [in the United States], it was not completed. It was prevented [and] was foiled." 764 is an extremist network that's been flagged by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation as a "tier one" threat. The group uses blackmail and manipulation to coerce minors into self-harm and explicit acts. It typically operates in decentralized platforms like Discord and Telegram to exploit minors on a global scale. Whether the Tacloban attack is the network's first completed shooting remains unproven, and Redoble and other authorities present at the inquiry stressed repeatedly that the link to 764 was not yet confirmed. Redoble told the committee his earlier research had pointed to groomers of the network mainly based abroad. But that was until foiled attacks in Marikina and Laguna suggested recruiters of 764 were already operating inside the country. When news of the Tacloban shooting broke, he said, his first questions were whether the attackers were gamers and whether the case was tied to 764, both of which, he said, appeared to hold up. Pressed by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on whether such groomers were already active in the country, Redoble pointed to a comment left on the Facebook page of one of the Tacloban suspects after the shooting, in which the user told the boy his footage had been edited and told him to delete his accounts. Redoble was referring to the comment of a certain "Sedykh Ryazanov" on one of the Facebook posts of the teenage gunman given the alias "Nash." A screengrab shown by Sen. Risa Hontiveros during the hearing shows that the user wrote: "Na-edit na kita boy sa TikTok. Make sure na-delete mo ang Discord, Reddit, Telegram para walang evidence mahanap." The accounts have since been deactivated, Hontiveros said. "That will confirm that we have a local player, a groomer or a recruiter that's operating in our own cyberspace," Redoble said. "Before we had patterns, but today I think we can say that we already have this players, and I don't think that guy is alone. I think there's more." Schools have no way of knowing how many of their students play games heavily or are being groomed, he said, and authorities should assume local recruiters are active. 764 changed its own rules in 2025, Redoble said, after a leadership shake-up inside the network. A recruit once had to produce child sexual abuse material to get in. Now, Redoble said the group demands proof of real-world violence. That rule, he said, is what turns groomed children into attackers. The predators or groomers also worked in stages, where they would first identify a vulnerable minor, befriend them, then cut them off from family before pushing them toward self-harm or an attack. "It's not the online game," Redoble said. "It's the perpetrators or the predators in the game that's really changing our children." He named three "hunting grounds" where recruiters look for children: mental-health support chats, online games, and a TikTok subculture built around Gothic fashion that draws teenage girls. Games including Roblox, Minecraft and Gorebox are where children are first spotted, he said, with the platforms' own recommendation systems steering vulnerable users toward one another. At least 24 minors have been rescued by the police from the same broad network since October, the PNP's anti-cybercrime group said during the hearing. Police Col. Richmond L. Tadina of the PNP's anti-cybercrime group said all 24 are part of the "True Crime Community." "We have identified No Lives Matter and the 764 network as subcultures. They are under the True Crime Community," Tadina said. "What is common is there is coercion, self-harm, exploitation of minors, and violence," he added. Five of the 24 minors rescued had "resorted to inflicting harm on themselves," Tadina said, due to their exposure to gore, including on the game GoreBox. Police were able to stop those 24 children from carrying out violence on others, he said. "So na-prevent po namin 'yung 24 minors to carry out violence," Tadina said. "However, it's sad to note that itong recent shooting is hindi natin na-prevent." The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center has temporarily blocked Gorebox, a physics-based sandbox game, which one of the Tacloban suspects played heavily. The Germany-based developer, Felix Filip, declined the committee's invitation to appear on Wednesday, telling the Senate panel by email that the game is rated 18+ and "not intended for, or directed at, minors." Hontiveros called the hearing to examine gun access, the police response to the Tacloban shooting and how online platforms are used to groom and radicalize children. It followed the committee's April inquiry into online radicalization, which pushed Roblox to tighten its safeguards for young users in the Philippines. output.title: Do video games cause violence? Tacloban shooting triggers debate | ABS-CBN News
output.description: The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are
output.text: MANILA — The government's temporary ban on the video game GoreBox following the deadly Tacloban school shooting has triggered a wider debate over whether video games are being unfairly blamed for a much deeper problem. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) temporarily blocked access to GoreBox after investigators found that one of the teenage suspects regularly played the game. The June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School left three students dead and 20 others injured, one of the deadliest school shootings in recent Philippine history. But while authorities investigate possible links, experts interviewed on DZMM and ANC warned against drawing a straight line between playing violent games and committing violent crimes. NO EVIDENCE OF LINK Scam Watch Pilipinas co-convenor and cybersecurity journalist Art Samaniego Jr., speaking on DZMM's Balitapatan, pointed to academic research showing no proven causal relationship between violent video games and criminal violence. "May ginawang study kasi sa Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford, na wala silang nakita clear link between aggressive behavior sa mga teenager at sa amount of time at kung anong nilalaro nila online." (The Oxford Internet Institute found no clear link between aggressive behavior among teenagers and the amount of time they spend playing online games or the type of games they play.) He went further. "Walang study na nagpapatunay na yung games nakaka-effect sa real life behavior ng gamer. Pero mayroong study nagpapatunay na walang effect ito sa real life behavior nung naglalaro." GoreBox screencap from Google Play (There is no study proving that games affect a gamer's real-life behavior. In fact, there are studies showing they do not affect real-life behavior.) The distinction is crucial because GoreBox itself has more than 10 million downloads worldwide on Google Play and carries a Mature 18+ rating, yet only a tiny fraction of players engage in real-world violence. 'THE GAME MAY NOT BE THE STORY' Instead of focusing solely on GoreBox, Samaniego urged authorities to examine the online communities that young people interact with. "Ito ang pinaka-importante na nakikita ko ngayon, online community na sinasalihan ng mga batang 'to." (What I think is most important right now is the online communities these children are joining.) He cited reports that investigators were looking into possible links between minors and extremist online networks such as the so-called "764" ecosystem, which has drawn scrutiny from international law enforcement agencies over allegations of grooming, coercion, self-harm encouragement, and youth radicalization. "Meron bang nag-uujok sa mga batang 'to na gawin ito?" (Was someone encouraging these children to do this?) Akbayan Party-list Rep. Chel Diokno said authorities should investigate not only games but also the individuals and networks that may be influencing children online. GoreBox screencap from Google Play "There must also be a thorough investigation into this because it is very concerning that there are not just online websites like that, but people operating in other countries who are apparently targeting young people," Diokno said. "We need to have a comprehensive investigation. We have to look at not just the online activities, but all the different angles." CICC: GOREBOX BAN COULD BECOME PERMANENT For the CICC, however, the immediate priority is preventing another tragedy while the investigation continues. Speaking to ANC, CICC Executive Director and Undersecretary Aboy Paraiso revealed that authorities had not previously monitored GoreBox despite its global popularity. "To be honest, we haven't paid any attention to this particular game. In fact, this is the first time we heard about the game." Paraiso said investigators became alarmed after learning the game may have been used as a "simulation" platform by one of the suspects. "This game has an extreme visual, gory content that leaves very little to the imagination." He noted that GoreBox combines graphic violence with simplified, block-style visuals that may appeal to younger audiences despite its mature rating. The CICC is now reviewing other gaming platforms and says the temporary block could become permanent. "If they fail to show that the game has age-appropriate content, they can verify the age, then this temporary ban becomes permanent." The controversy surrounding GoreBox has become one of the most closely watched technology and child-safety issues in the Philippines this year, raising questions about violent video games, online radicalization, youth mental health, internet regulation, and the role of parents, schools, technology companies and government in protecting children online. GoreBox, developed by Germany-based F2Games, allows players to experiment with firearms, explosives and other weapons in an open-world environment. The game describes itself as "a physics-driven sandbox game where creativity meets unrestrained destruction." GoreBox screencap from Google Play According to the CICC, the title is known for graphic depictions of violence and highly detailed injury effects that leave "very little to the imagination." Meanwhile, the game itself has very blocky animation, similar to Roblox and Minecraft, unlike other popular shooting games with realistic graphics. F2Games did not immediately respond to media requests for comment following the Philippine government's decision to block access to the game. A REGULATORY GAP The Tacloban case has also exposed what government officials describe as a major regulatory blind spot. Paraiso admitted that Philippine authorities currently have limited power over foreign-based gaming, social media and messaging platforms. "There has to be some legislative intervention right now because there's no legal basis for us to regulate these games." "We have no jurisdiction over these games, gaming platforms, social media platforms, even messaging platforms." He said lawmakers should consider legislation that would give Philippine authorities greater authority over platforms operating in the country. GROWING REGIONAL SCRUTINY OF CHILDREN'S ONLINE ACTIVITY The Philippine government's action against GoreBox comes as countries across the Asia-Pacific region impose stricter controls on children's online activity amid concerns over cyberbullying, harmful content, online grooming, radicalization, and excessive screen time. In March, Indonesia began enforcing restrictions on social media and gaming accounts for users under 16. Malaysia has introduced mandatory age verification requirements for social media users, while Australia last year enacted legislation restricting social media access for children younger than 16. The Philippines is now confronting similar questions following the Tacloban school shooting: How should governments balance child safety with access to technology, education and online communities? For CICC Executive Director Aboy Paraiso, the answer cannot rely solely on bans. "There has to be some legislative intervention right now because there's no legal basis for us to regulate these games." At the same time, experts warn that regulation should be evidence-based. While violent games have periodically faced restrictions around the world—including temporary actions against titles or platforms over concerns ranging from violence to child safety—researchers continue to debate whether such measures reduce real-world violence. That is why Samaniego and Diokno argue that authorities should look beyond the game itself and investigate online ecosystems, extremist networks, mental health concerns, bullying, family environments, and other factors that may contribute to youth violence. LESSONS FROM OTHER COUNTRIES The Philippines is not the first country to restrict or ban digital platforms over concerns involving minors. Governments in several countries have imposed restrictions on games or gaming platforms for reasons ranging from violent content and extremism to child safety concerns. Most recently, Russia blocked access to Roblox, citing harmful content concerns, while Roblox itself has repeatedly removed user-created simulations of school shootings and extremist content. But experts caution that bans alone rarely address underlying drivers of violence. INTERNET SAFETY FROM GRADE 1? One proposal drawing broad support is integrating digital literacy and internet safety into basic education. Samaniego welcomed CICC proposals to introduce online safety lessons in schools. "Kaya ang saya ko nung sinabi ng CICC Director Aboy Paraiso na i-recommend niya isama ang internet safety sa kurikulum ng eskwelahan." (I was happy when CICC Director Aboy Paraiso said he would recommend including internet safety in the school curriculum.) He argued that online safety education should start much earlier. "Grade 1 pa lang, turuan na natin. Kasi pag umabot na grade 6 baka too late na." (We should start teaching this as early as Grade 1. By Grade 6, it may already be too late.) Paraiso likewise stressed that technology, parenting, education, and legislation must all work together. "It's sad that these events have to happen," he said. For both supporters and critics of the GoreBox ban, one point appears increasingly clear: the conversation is no longer just about a video game. It is about how children navigate an online world where games, chat groups, social media platforms, extremist networks, and real-life grievances can intersect in ways that are still poorly understood.
